_note: Second reading of AI reader 110's anchors (the day after: alcohol, 8 PMC papers).

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Results › Memory › Short-term memory
tasks.locator: Results › Memory › Short-term memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend
tasks.extracted: Seven studies measured short-term memory: three reported impairment (one in women only) and four did not; pooled over five studies, Hedges' g = 0.64 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.13), I2 = 73%, P = 0.01, worse after heavy drinking.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Results › Memory › Long-term memory
tasks.locator: Results › Memory › Long-term memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 5 legend
tasks.extracted: Four studies measured long-term memory: the three word-recall studies found impairment and the study in which material was learned while sober did not; pooled g = 0.59 (0.01 to 1.17), I2 = 84%, P = 0.05.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Results › Attention › Sustained attention
tasks.locator: Results › Attention › Sustained attention, 1st paragraph; Figure 3 legend
tasks.extracted: Five studies measured sustained attention (three laboratory, two naturalistic): three reported impairment and two did not; pooled over four studies, g = 0.47 (0.07 to 0.87), I2 = 50%, P = 0.02.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Results › Psychomotor performance › Speed
tasks.locator: Results › Psychomotor performance › Speed, 1st paragraph; Figure 6 legend; Discussion, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Reaction time was slower in three naturalistic studies and unchanged in three laboratory studies; pooled over five studies, g = 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00), I2 = 36%, P < 0.001. One laboratory study with no change in reaction time could not be pooled, which the authors say may inflate the estimate.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Results › Attention › Divided attention; Results › Memory › Other memory; Results › 'Real-life' simulations
tasks.locator: Results › Attention › Divided attention, 1st paragraph; Results › Memory › Other memory, 1st paragraph; Results › 'Real-life' simulations, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Divided attention: only one of five studies (n = 5) found impairment, and the meta-analysis of four showed no evidence of an effect (no estimate given). Working memory was mixed (impairment on one of three tasks in one study). No clear effect on a ship power-plant problem, managerial simulations or examination scores.

tasks.locator: Introduction, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors state that people in the hangover conditions may have had no symptoms, so the review examines next-day effects of heavy drinking rather than hangover as such; that naturalistic studies, with more alcohol, were more likely to find impairment; and that condition and task order were not always randomized, nicotine was not always controlled and the sleep allowed varied between studies.

tasks.locator: Table 1, Divided Attention › Mean Response Time row; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: During a simulated commute, divided-attention response time was slower on the morning after a night of social drinking than after a night without alcohol: 3.5 (SD 1.8) against 2.4 (1.3) in all 52 drivers, d = 0.55, and 3.4 (1.6) against 2.3 (1.0) in the 26 with zero breath alcohol, d = 0.69 (F(1,50) = 15.6, p < 0.0001).

tasks.locator: Table 1, Combined Groups columns; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: In all 52 drivers, eight of 15 driving measures were worse on the morning after drinking: divided-attention response time 3.5 (SD 1.8) against 2.4 (1.3), d = 0.55; incorrect and missed responses d = 0.21 and 0.30; mean speed 35.9 against 31.7 mph, d = 0.42; centre-line crossings 7.8% against 4.0%, d = 0.36; time off road 1.6% against 0.6%, d = 0.68; lane excursions 18.9 against 10.6, d = 0.58; tickets 1.2 against 0.8, d = 0.34.

tasks.locator: Table 1, Zero BAC Group columns; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: In the 26 drivers with zero breath alcohol: response time 3.4 against 2.3, d = 0.69; mean speed 33.7 against 29.1 mph, d = 0.40; centre-line crossings 6.0% against 3.8%, d = 0.48; time off road 1.3% against 0.5%, d = 0.61; lane excursions 20.2 against 9.7, d = 0.64; collisions 1.1 against 1.6, not significant.

tasks.locator: Table 1, Lane Deviation, Speed Deviation, Mean Lane Position, Accidents and Collisions and Speed Limit Exceedances rows
tasks.extracted: Lane deviation (2.9 against 2.6), speed variability, mean lane position, collisions (1.8 against 1.3) and speed-limit exceedances did not differ significantly between the two mornings in all 52 drivers; lane deviation is the measure closest to the standard highway test.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 (Residual Alcohol Group); Results › 3.1
tasks.locator: Table 1, Control and Hangover columns of the Zero BAC and Residual Alcohol groups; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Drivers with residual breath alcohol had more collisions on the morning after drinking (2.5 against 0.9, d = 0.74), the only measure with an alcohol-by-group interaction. They also drove faster, exceeded speed limits more and got more tickets than the zero group, but they did so on the alcohol-free morning too (34.3 against 29.1 mph; 10.4 against 7.0 exceedances; 1.0 against 0.6 tickets), so these group differences are not effects of residual alcohol.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st, 6th and 8th paragraphs; Results › 3 (opening paragraph)
tasks.extracted: Drinking was unobserved and amounts are not reported (some participants could not recall them); sleep was not recorded, and the authors name sleep loss as a likely part of the effect. Their statement that the impairment equals driving over a legal blood alcohol limit cites another study's highway test; no alcohol benchmark was run in this study.

tasks.locator: Results › 'Real-life' simulations, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Of three naturalistic studies of driving the morning after heavy drinking, two found poorer control of the vehicle (deviation from a set course; Laurell and Törnros, 1983; Verster et al., 2014) and one found no next-day effect on speed (Törnros and Laurell, 1991); differences in method prevented pooling.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend
tasks.extracted: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde did not differ significantly between the water and no-water sessions at any time after drinking; acetaldehyde point estimates were slightly higher with water shortly after drinking, and the curves were almost identical by the next morning.

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (last sentence); Figure 4
tasks.extracted: None of the six visual analogue ratings (facial flushing, headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness, feeling exhilarated) differed significantly between the sessions at any time point; values are shown only in figures.

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3; Discussions, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Digit Symbol Substitution Test change from baseline was lower with water right after drinking (p = 0.01), which the authors link to abdominal bloating from the large amount of fluid, and higher with water at the first two next-morning tests (p = 0.05 and 0.08), described as not statistically significant.

tasks.locator: Discussions, 4th and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors state that with 13 participants power was barely 0.8 for an effect size of 1, that all were men of one genotype, that the open-label design may have biased the ratings, and that the design cannot separate water between drinks from drinking the alcohol diluted.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Funding Statement; Conflict of interests; Author contributions
tasks.locator: Funding Statement; Conflict of interests; Author contributions
tasks.extracted: Funded by the sake brewer that made the test drink; four of eight authors were employed by its research laboratory, two of whom did the formal analysis, although the funding statement says the funder had no role in analysis.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Primary outcome: total Hangover Symptoms Scale score did not differ between NAC and placebo (median 10 against 13, P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum); headache (1 against 1, P = 0.93), nausea (0 against 1, P = 0.11) and weakness (1 against 1, P = 0.72) did not differ either.

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 1
tasks.extracted: A subset of five validated items gave the same result: median 5 (range 0 to 19) with NAC against 5.5 (0 to 20) with placebo, P = 0.86 (analysed as independent groups, with 91 of 98 expected observations).

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Difference scores (NAC minus placebo) were −3.5 in women and +2 in men (P = 0.04), with sex differences for nausea (P = 0.05) and weakness (P = 0.03) but not headache (P = 0.32); the Discussion calls the symptom comparisons post hoc.

tasks.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Side effects attributed to the pill: after NAC, gastrointestinal symptoms (4), headache (2), rash (1), muscle twitches (1) and insomnia (1); after placebo, headache (3) and gastrointestinal symptoms (1); no serious adverse events.

tasks.locator: Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: 62 enrolled and 49 completed. The authors name as limitations the low doses, supervised sessions that ended at a breath alcohol target and may have produced milder hangovers than unrestricted drinking, possible drinking after leaving, and unsupervised completion of the scale at home.

tasks.locator: Table 2, Acute Hangover Scale score and Hangover incidence rows; Results › Hangover, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Hangover severity 1.34 (SD 0.84) with caffeine against 1.45 (0.89) without, d = 0.13; any hangover 60.7% against 69.4%, h = 0.19; neither significant (n = 28 and 36).

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Table 2; Results › 2.5 Subjective Sleep Quality and Morning Sleepiness
tasks.locator: Table 2; Results › 2.5 Subjective Sleep Quality and Morning Sleepiness, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Self-reported minutes to fall asleep (36.5 against 23.2), minutes asleep (390.7 against 404.7) and Stanford Sleepiness (2.52 against 2.78) did not differ significantly (d = 0.28, 0.21, 0.23).

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.5 Subjective Sleep Quality and Morning Sleepiness
tasks.locator: Results › 2.5 Subjective Sleep Quality and Morning Sleepiness, 1st paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: The caffeine group rated average sleep quality better (4.45, SD 0.41, against 4.16, SD 0.49; t(62) = 2.49; d = 0.64); split afterwards, the difference lay more in morning alertness and concentration items (d = 0.42, p < 0.10) than in night-time items (d = 0.30).

tasks.page: PMC HTML, 1. Introduction; Results › 2.4 Participant characteristics; 3. Discussion
tasks.locator: 1. Introduction, 5th paragraph; Results › 2.4 Participant characteristics, 1st paragraph; 3. Discussion, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: A secondary analysis of a randomized trial designed to study driving, comparing its two alcohol groups (completers only, 28 and 36); the authors acknowledge low power and that results may differ with other amounts of alcohol or caffeine and with older people.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity; Figure 3
tasks.locator: Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3
tasks.extracted: The within-person difference in hangover score between drinking orders was −0.32 (SD 7.63) in study group 1 and 0.36 (SD 6.82) in study group 2 (31 each), P = 0.71; none of the three groups had a significantly different score with a different order or drink, including controls drinking beer only on one day and wine only on the other.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Sample size; Results › Study population
tasks.locator: Methods › Sample size; Results › Study population, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The trial was planned to detect a 14% difference (1 point on each of 8 items) with 80% power, targeting 36 per study group; 105 were randomized and 90 completed (31, 31 and 28), losses being mostly due to exams or holidays.

tasks.page: PMC HTML, Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity; Figure 5
tasks.locator: Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 5 legend
tasks.extracted: In exploratory regressions with backward selection, vomiting and perceived drunkenness were associated with higher hangover scores on both days; women reported more severe hangovers than men (P = 0.009), a tendency that remained, not significantly, after dividing by peak breath alcohol.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors note that only a lager and a white wine were used, that blinding beer and wine proved impossible, and that an alcohol-free control group was not feasible.

tasks.locator: Table 1; Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Of 1312 past-month drinkers aged 21 to 24, 42 (3.2%) had ever used hangover remedy pills, 248 (18.9%) had heard of them and 110 (8.6%) believed they work.

tasks.locator: Table 2, Alcohol use problem score, drinks per typical drinking day and Past Year AUD symptom count rows; Results, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The ever-use group scored higher on the modified AUDIT (7.7 against 5.4; adjusted B = 2.29, 95% CI 0.82 to 3.76), drank more per drinking day (adjusted rate ratio 1.24, 1.02 to 1.49) and reported more alcohol-related problems (1.7 against 0.9 of 7; adjusted rate ratio 1.86, 1.18 to 3.02, also adjusted for drinking frequency and intensity).

tasks.locator: Table 2, drinking days and binge drinking days rows; Discussion, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Ever-use was not detectably associated with drinking days (adjusted rate ratio 1.19, 0.94 to 1.51) or binge-drinking days (1.40, 0.91 to 2.23).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Methods › Measures › Hangover remedy use
tasks.extracted: A single yes-or-no item asked about ever using hangover remedy pills; the authors state that causal interpretation is not possible, that ever-use does not separate recent from past or occasional from regular use, and that the small number who had used pills limits power.

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 1; Figure 2 legend
tasks.extracted: Five trials (551 on acetaminophen, 350 on placebo) were pooled with a fixed-effect model: the difference in mean change in ALT is printed as 0.0 IU/L (95% CI −0.2 to 0.1), Q = 1.7, I2 = 0. Recalculated from Table 1, these figures are a standardized difference (−0.04, −0.17 to 0.10), as the forest-plot legend says; in IU/L the pooled difference is 0.09 (−1.27 to 1.46) (editors' calculation).

tasks.locator: Results, 1st, 5th and 7th paragraphs; Abstract › Main Results
tasks.extracted: No randomized trial, included or excluded, reported liver dysfunction, liver failure or death; AST, INR, bilirubin and glutathione S-transferase changes were similar between groups where reported, apart from a rise in INR in people taking warfarin.

tasks.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: At later, unpooled measurements ALT was higher with acetaminophen than placebo by 12.6 IU/L (Dart 2010) and 8.4 IU/L (Heard 2007, statistically significant), mostly just after the end of dosing, and by 18.7 and 8.1 IU/L at the higher and lower dose in a trial of people taking warfarin (Parra 2007), with no difference at that trial's last measurement.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
tasks.extracted: Four of the six included trials (four of the five pooled) enrolled people with heavy drinking admitted to detoxification, who started acetaminophen soon after their last drink and had no alcohol during the trial; one enrolled moderate drinkers who kept drinking. In two pooled trials dosing had ended before the pooled measurement.

tasks.locator: Methods, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Footnotes › Financial disclosure; References 6 to 10
tasks.extracted: The protocol was not registered and no assessment of bias in the trials was done. The review was funded by an investigator-initiated grant from McNeil Consumer Healthcare, which reviewed the manuscript; one author had consulted and testified for McNeil; review authors are authors of all five pooled trials.
